scenes.tts: In the first film, an open channel spent ion gradients to swing membrane voltage in a millisecond. So what opens that gate? And how can a second lock or a plug stop ions passing?

scenes.visual: Reuses the exact membrane world and colour map from the first film: deep slate (#0F172A), horizontal bilayer (Outside above, Inside below), drifting amber Na+, teal K+, violet Ca2+, and the right-hand vertical voltage gauge with white Vm needle at rest (−70 mV). Zoom smoothly onto a closed silver-blue channel gate pulsing gently at centre.

scenes.visual: Hold the gently drifting membrane world dimmed behind high-contrast white title text (size 48): 'Gates, Two Locks, and Plugs'. Ions keep drifting slowly in the background.

scenes.tts: A signal acts by opening the gate, so the gate is what makes a channel a receptor. Gates answer three main keys. The first key is a chemical ligand. A neurotransmitter docks outside the channel, twisting the gate open so ions flow. Other channels answer messengers inside the cell instead.
scenes.caption: A signal acts by opening the gate, so the gate is what makes a channel a receptor. Gates answer three main keys. The first key is a chemical ligand. A neurotransmitter docks outside the channel, twisting the gate open so ions flow. Other channels answer messengers inside the cell instead.
scenes.visual: Same membrane and voltage gauge. Label top left: 'Key 1: Ligand'. A bright ligand shape docks onto an outer binding pocket of the channel; the channel hinges smoothly open and amber Na+ streams in as the Vm needle rises. Then a brief morph highlights a binding pocket on the inner face receiving an intracellular messenger tag so the gate opens from below.
scenes.narration: A signal acts by opening the gate, so the gate is what makes a channel a receptor. Gates answer three main keys. The first key is a chemical ligand. A neurotransmitter docks outside the channel, twisting the gate open so ions flow. Other channels answer messengers inside the cell instead.

scenes.tts: The second key is membrane voltage itself. Voltage-gated sodium, potassium, and calcium channels carry four voltage sensors. Each sensor holds a helix called S four, studded with positive charges. Membrane voltage creates an electric field. Depolarise the cell, and that field pushes S four outward, pulling the gate open.
scenes.caption: The second key is membrane voltage itself. Voltage-gated Na+, K+, and Ca2+ channels carry four voltage sensors. Each sensor holds a helix called S4, studded with positive charges. Membrane voltage creates an electric field. Depolarise the cell, and that field pushes S4 outward, pulling the gate open.
scenes.visual: The same channel morphs cleanly in place into a voltage-gated channel (label 'Key 2: Voltage'). Flanking the central pore sit highlighted S4 helices marked with glowing '+' signs. As a small upward nudge lifts the right-hand Vm needle (less negative inside), electric-field arrows push the '+'-studded S4 helices outward, levering the central gate wide open.
scenes.narration: The second key is membrane voltage itself. Voltage-gated Na+, K+, and Ca2+ channels carry four voltage sensors. Each sensor holds a helix called S4, studded with positive charges. Membrane voltage creates an electric field. Depolarise the cell, and that field pushes S4 outward, pulling the gate open.

scenes.tts: That lets voltage-gated sodium channels feed back on themselves. Entering sodium depolarises the membrane further, opening more channels in a fast pulse, the nerve impulse. The third key comes from the outside world. A physical stimulus, such as heat, can open a sensory channel’s gate directly.
scenes.caption: That lets voltage-gated Na+ channels feed back on themselves. Entering Na+ depolarises the membrane further, opening more channels in a fast pulse, the nerve impulse. The third key comes from the outside world. A physical stimulus, such as heat, can open a sensory channel’s gate directly.
scenes.visual: First, two neighbouring amber-trimmed Na+ channels appear along the bilayer: amber Na+ enters the first, lifting the Vm needle and popping the neighbouring gate open in a chain reaction (label 'Positive feedback'). Then the frame focuses back on one channel (label 'Key 3: Physical stimulus'): warm wavy heat lines wash over the membrane and smoothly swing the sensory gate open.

scenes.tts: Some receptors conduct strongly only when two events coincide. At synapses, the junctions between nerve cells, the N M D A receptor sits beside A M P A glutamate receptors. With glutamate bound, plus glycine or D-serine, its gate opens. Yet magnesium ions wait outside.
scenes.caption: Some receptors conduct strongly only when two events coincide. At synapses, the junctions between nerve cells, the NMDA receptor sits beside AMPA glutamate receptors. With glutamate bound, plus glycine or D-serine, its gate opens. Yet Mg2+ ions wait outside.
scenes.visual: Same membrane world, voltage gauge back at rest (−70 mV). Left: a compact channel labelled 'AMPA receptor'. Right: a taller channel labelled 'NMDA receptor' (with small outer pockets marked 'Glutamate' and 'Glycine / D-serine'). Above the membrane, amber Na+, violet Ca2+, and lime-green Mg2+ ions drift. Glutamate and glycine dock on the NMDA receptor and its gate opens.
scenes.narration: Some receptors conduct strongly only when two events coincide. At synapses, the junctions between nerve cells, the NMDA receptor sits beside AMPA glutamate receptors. With glutamate bound, plus glycine or D-serine, its gate opens. Yet Mg2+ ions wait outside.

scenes.tts: Now hold the neuron at rest, electrically negative inside, while glutamate opens that receptor’s gate. Pause and predict. Why does almost no current flow through this open channel?
scenes.caption: Now hold the neuron at rest, electrically negative inside, while glutamate opens that receptor’s gate. Pause and predict. Why does almost no current flow through this open channel?
scenes.visual: Keep the NMDA receptor on screen with glutamate bound and its gate visibly open, the right-hand Vm needle held at resting negative voltage (−70 mV), and lime-green Mg2+ drifting near the pore mouth. A clean prompt card appears at top: 'Predict: Why is current nearly zero?'
scenes.narration: Now hold the neuron at rest, electrically negative inside, while glutamate opens that receptor’s gate. Pause and predict. Why does almost no current flow through this open channel?

scenes.visual: Hold the prompt card, open-gated NMDA receptor, hovering lime-green Mg2+, and steady resting Vm needle on screen. Ions keep drifting slowly; a thin progress bar moves across the bottom of the prompt card.

scenes.tts: Magnesium is positive, so the negative inside pulls it into the open pore, where it sticks and blocks flow. Now let nearby glutamate receptors open. Sodium enters and depolarises the membrane. With the inside less negative, the pull weakens and magnesium is driven back out. Sodium and calcium pour in. So two events must coincide: glutamate released, and the cell already depolarised.
scenes.caption: Mg2+ is positive, so the negative inside pulls it into the open pore, where it sticks and blocks flow. Now let nearby glutamate receptors open. Na+ enters and depolarises the membrane. With the inside less negative, the pull weakens and Mg2+ is driven back out. Na+ and Ca2+ pour in. So two events must coincide: glutamate released, and the cell already depolarised.
scenes.visual: Prompt card clears. A lime-green Mg2+ ion snaps down into the open NMDA pore like a cork; amber Na+ and violet Ca2+ bounce off it (label 'Mg2+ block at rest'). Next, the neighbouring AMPA receptor opens: amber Na+ enters and pushes the white Vm needle upward. As voltage rises, the lime-green Mg2+ pops out upward, and a bright stream of amber Na+ and violet Ca2+ floods into the cell.
scenes.narration: Mg2+ is positive, so the negative inside pulls it into the open pore, where it sticks and blocks flow. Now let nearby glutamate receptors open. Na+ enters and depolarises the membrane. With the inside less negative, the pull weakens and Mg2+ is driven back out. Na+ and Ca2+ pour in. So two events must coincide: glutamate released, and the cell already depolarised.

scenes.tts: Because a channel is a hole, toxins and drugs can plug it. Tetrodotoxin lodges in the outer mouth of nerve and muscle sodium channels, so sodium cannot enter and no impulse starts. Ketamine enters an open N M D A pore to block it from within. It also makes the channel open less often.
scenes.caption: Because a channel is a hole, toxins and drugs can plug it. Tetrodotoxin lodges in the outer mouth of nerve and muscle Na+ channels, so Na+ cannot enter and no impulse starts. Ketamine enters an open NMDA pore to block it from within. It also makes the channel open less often.
scenes.visual: Split the carried bilayer neatly into two side-by-side channels using the exact same colours. Left: a voltage-gated Na+ channel; a coral-red plug (#F43F5E) labelled 'Tetrodotoxin' wedges into the outer mouth, bouncing amber Na+ away while the Vm needle stays flat at rest. Right: an open NMDA receptor; a coral-red wedge labelled 'Ketamine' enters deep inside the open pore, stopping amber Na+ and violet Ca2+ flow.
scenes.narration: Because a channel is a hole, toxins and drugs can plug it. Tetrodotoxin lodges in the outer mouth of nerve and muscle Na+ channels, so Na+ cannot enter and no impulse starts. Ketamine enters an open NMDA pore to block it from within. It also makes the channel open less often.

scenes.tts: Together, gates and pore blocks turn simple holes into sharp switches. Ligands, voltage, or physical stimuli open the gate. Then voltage-sensitive magnesium, a toxin, or a drug determines whether ions get through. Signals open the gate, and pore blocks control whether ions pass.
scenes.caption: Together, gates and pore blocks turn simple holes into sharp switches. Ligands, voltage, or physical stimuli open the gate. Then voltage-sensitive Mg2+, a toxin, or a drug determines whether ions get through. Signals open the gate, and pore blocks control whether ions pass.
scenes.visual: Return to a single clean view of the carried channel in the bilayer with two crisp callouts pulsing sequentially: 'Gate' (briefly cycling ligand, S4 voltage, and heat icons) and 'Pore block' (briefly cycling lime Mg2+ and coral-red blocker). Ions stream cleanly when the gate is open and the pore is clear, then fade toward the end card.
scenes.narration: Together, gates and pore blocks turn simple holes into sharp switches. Ligands, voltage, or physical stimuli open the gate. Then voltage-sensitive Mg2+, a toxin, or a drug determines whether ions get through. Signals open the gate, and pore blocks control whether ions pass.
